activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The nucleus in an onion cell shows up as a small, round, darker spot, and it holds the cell's genetic material, DNA.
story:
Jasmine set the microscope on the kitchen table exactly the way Ms. Banerjee's note had described, because the note was all she had. "Bring your slide back Monday," it read in Ms. Banerjee's tidy handwriting, "and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. Careful with the focus knob. Do not modify the settings I marked with tape." The tape was still there, two green strips on the coarse knob, so Jasmine only touched the fine one.

Teagan sat across from her, chin on her hands. She had brought the onions, three of them, because she wanted first look. "I'm basically nocturnal during swim season," she said, "so a Friday night microscope party is perfect for me. But I get to see the cells before you draw them. That's my price."

"Deal," Jasmine said, though she regretted it the moment the light snapped on.

Under the lens the onion skin looked like a brick wall made of living things, each cell a tidy rectangle. Teagan took her turn first, as promised, and hogged the eyepiece for a full minute. "There are little dark dots," she reported. "Like somebody sneezed pepper on it."

Jasmine's stomach dropped. Ms. Banerjee wanted the nucleus labeled, and if the dots were dirt, she would label a speck of dust on her drawing and hand in a mistake for the whole class to see. She thought about it while Teagan kept looking. Dirt would land wherever it landed, in clumps, in streaks, in some cells and not others. She leaned in and checked. One dot per cell. Every single rectangle had its own small, round, darker spot, sitting there like it belonged.

"That's not dirt," Jasmine said slowly. "Dirt wouldn't be so neat. That dot is the nucleus. It's in every cell because every cell needs it. It holds the DNA."

"What's DNA?" Teagan asked.

"The genetic material. Like the instructions for the whole onion."

She drew the cells on graph paper, wall on the outside, membrane drawn just inside it, nucleus as its careful round dot. Her labeling was going to be the best in the class. Then she remembered the deal and slid the paper aside so Teagan could copy the shapes too, which meant Teagan's Monday would look almost as good, and Jasmine's mom called down that lights out was in ten minutes, before she could label the last three cells.

Teagan grinned and picked up the pencil herself. "I'll do these ones," she said. "I'm the nocturnal one, after all."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: If a knife starts to fall, step back and let it drop; trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut.
story:
Dylan had signed up for the Saturday shift at the community kitchen because his grandmother used to volunteer there after she retired, back when her pension was small and the work made her feel useful. Now he stood at a steel counter beside Zac and Kathryn, six onions in front of him and a note card from the coordinator in his pocket. The card read: "Dylan, you're on sauce today. Mr. Romano will show you the knife work. Chop small, cook slow, and the soup line eats at noon." He read it twice, because noon sounded very close.

Mr. Romano put a chef's knife in Dylan's hand and an onion on the cutting board. "Claw grip," he said, curling Dylan's fingertips under so only the knuckles faced the blade. "The knife rides against your knuckles. The fingertips stay out of the way." Dylan pressed down and the onion split with a crack, and the smell hit him right away, sharp enough to make his eyes water. He kept his wrist moving the tip in a smooth rock, the way Mr. Romano had shown, and the cubes came out small and fairly consistent, all about the same size, which apparently mattered because they would cook at the same rate.

Zac was on garlic at the next board. Halfway through his pile he reached for a bowl at the back of the counter and his elbow knocked the handle of his knife. The blade slid off the edge. Zac's hand shot out to grab it.

Dylan had seen this before. Last summer at the lake, a kid named nothing anyone remembered now had swept a paring knife off a picnic table reaching for marshmallows, snatched at it midair, and opened a gash across three fingers that ruined the whole trip and meant a long drive to the clinic. Dylan had stood there watching it happen and done nothing. This time he grabbed Zac's sleeve and yanked him back a step. The knife hit the floor handle first, bounced, and lay still. Nobody was bleeding.

"Sorry," Zac said. "Instinct."

"That's how people get cut," Dylan said. "You just step back and let it drop."

Mr. Romano picked the knife up, checked the edge, and set it down flat on the board. "Falling knife, empty hands," he said, and went back to the stove.

Kathryn had the tomatoes going in the big pot, and the kitchen filled with the smell of them collapsing into oil and onion, sweet and a little smoky where the bits on the bottom browned. Dylan stirred with a wooden spoon longer than he thought necessary, tasting at the end, adding a pinch of salt, tasting again. When the sauce finally tasted like something he would want on pasta, not like watery tomato, he understood why the note card said cook slow.

At noon the line formed. A man Dylan recognized from the bus stop took the first bowl and said the sauce was good, and a woman asked if there was extra for her neighbor. Mr. Romano told them the kitchen was able to donate twenty extra portions this week because the sauce had stretched farther than planned. Dylan washed the boards and knives at the sink, drying each blade and laying it flat, well back from the edge.

His grandmother had told him once that the kitchen would teach him more than chopping. He hadn't believed her, but he put her note card, the one she'd left him, back in his pocket next to the day's schedule, and carried the last pot to the line.

"Same time next Saturday?" Zac called after him.

"Bring your own knife," Dylan said. "Just don't catch it."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, the % operator gives the remainder of a division, so n % d == 0 is true exactly when d divides n evenly.
story:
Evan hunched over the team laptop behind the robotics table, typing and deleting the same line for the third time. The competition gym smelled like burnt coffee and floor wax, and in twenty minutes the judges would walk by to score their display station. Their robot worked fine. The trouble was the little quiz program Ms. Kang had suggested as a bonus station, a Python program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime, and Evan had promised he could build it.

"How's the wizard coming?" Thomas asked, sliding into the next chair. He wanted that bonus point badly, because his robot arm had jammed during the obstacle run and the quiz station was his only chance to impress the judges today. "Two minutes, I swear," Evan said, though his screen showed nothing but an input line and a blinking cursor. He knew primes were numbers that only divided by one and themselves. What he didn't know was how a program could possibly check whether a division came out even.

He typed a few guesses. If he divided 9 by 3, the answer was 3.0, and dividing 10 by 3 gave 3.3333333. Maybe he could turn the answer into letters and check for the dot? That felt wrong, and anyway it made his embarrassment flare hot enough that he was glad Thomas couldn't see the screen. Then he noticed a symbol in his notes from class, a percent sign, and an old line he had copied off the board: n % d == 0. "The percent operator gives the remainder of a division," he murmured, reading his own handwriting. So n % d == 0 was true exactly when d divided n evenly. Remainder zero meant nothing left over. That was the whole trick.

"Found something?" Thomas asked, leaning over. Evan typed fast, a loop that marched d from 2 up through the number, checking the remainder each time. "Try it," he said, spinning the laptop. Thomas entered 9 and the program printed PRIME, which was flatly wrong, and both boys groaned. Evan read his loop again and saw it: the loop stopped one number too early, so it never tested 3 itself. He fixed the range and ran it again. 9 printed NOT PRIME. 7 printed PRIME. His whole face went warm, but this time with something better.

When Ms. Kang stopped at their table, Evan was assertive in a way he never was in class. "You type in any number," he told the judge beside her, "and it tells you if it's prime." The judge entered 51. NOT PRIME, said the screen, and 51 divided by 3 was exactly 17, so it was right. Thomas pumped his fist and wrote their station number on the judge's clipboard himself.

Afterward, Thomas tried to reassure Evan about the earlier bug, saying nobody had seen it. Evan shook his head and pulled the laptop back. He entered 2, then 97, then 100, watching each answer appear. "One more," he said, and typed 997.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Buddhism teaches rebirth but denies a permanent soul, called anatta or no-self, so what continues from life to life is a chain of karma, not an unchanging self.
story:
The community hall smelled like paper and glue, and the folding tables had been pushed into a big circle so every group could show its project at the interfaith fair on Saturday. Aubrey had claimed the table nearest the window, which meant her poster got the best light but also the most glare, so she kept tilting it back and forth like it might magically fix itself.

"Our topic is what happens after death," said Nyla, reading the assignment card again, even though all three of them had it memorized. "Compare two faiths. We chose Hinduism and Buddhism because they're neighbors, right? Same part of the world, same basic idea."

"Rebirth," said Dario, tapping the word he had lettered across the top of the poster. "Both of them. The soul comes back in a new body. Done. We could be finished by tonight."

Aubrey frowned at the poster. Something about the word "soul" kept snagging on her, the way a sleeve catches on a door handle. She flipped through her notebook, where she had copied quotes from the library books before Mr. García unlocked the storage closet to get them more poster board.

"Wait," she said. "Look at this." She read aloud from her notes: "'Buddhism teaches rebirth but denies a permanent soul.'" She looked up. "Both things. At the same time."

Dario laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the glue. "That's like saying you get on the bus but there's no bus. How can something come back if there's nothing to come back?"

"Maybe it's a typo," said Nyla.

Aubrey didn't think it was a typo. Two different books said the same thing, and a typo doesn't happen twice in two books with the word spelled correctly. She stared at the blank space in the middle of their poster, where a diagram was supposed to go, and turned the problem over in her head. If nothing permanent crosses over, then what exactly is doing the crossing? She thought about the school assembly last month, where a candle flame had been passed along a whole row of candles for some ceremony nobody remembered the reason for now. Each flame lit the next one. No single flame traveled down the row. Each one was new, but the fire came from somewhere real.

She grabbed a candle from the supply box and three birthday candles from her backpack, leftover from Dario's little brother's party. "Watch," she said. She lit the big candle with a match, then used its flame to light the first small one, then used that one to light the second. She blew out the first small candle and held up the second, still burning.

"The second flame wasn't in the big candle," she said slowly, testing the idea as she said it. "But it came from it. Cause and effect, all the way down the line."

Nyla leaned in. "So Buddhism says that's what continues? Not a soul, but a chain? Like one action leads to the next life the way one flame lights the next?"

"That's karma," Aubrey said, checking her notes. "And there's a word for the no-soul part." She ran her finger down the page. "Anatta. It means no-self." Dario wrote the word on a card and propped it between the two candles, which were now orbiting each other faintly in the draft from the window whenever someone opened the door.

"So in Hinduism, a permanent soul travels," said Nyla, drawing an arrow with a stick figure riding on it, which made Dario snort. "And in Buddhism, no rider. Just the passing of the flame."

Mr. García came by with the sign-up sheet for Saturday's table assignments and stopped, one hand on his clipboard. "Candles at an interfaith fair," he said. "You three are a fire marshal's nightmare. Battery-operated ones only, and I'm afraid that's at your own expense, since the budget went to the microphone that keeps cutting out."

"We'll bring the flameless ones," Aubrey said. "But the diagram stays." She picked up the marker and began drawing the chain: candle, flame, candle, flame, all the way across the middle of the poster, a gradual line of small fires stretching from one edge to the other.

Dario tilted his head at it. "You know," he said, "that's either going to confuse everyone who walks by, or it's going to be the best thing in this whole hall."

"Both," said Nyla. "Definitely both."

Aubrey capped the marker and lit one more birthday candle off the survivor, just to watch it catch.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false.
story:
The challenge board outside the water lab said FIND WHAT BREAKS THE RULE, WIN THE PASSES, and Alex wanted those passes more than anything, because the passes meant the deep-sea dome, and the deep-sea dome closed for renovations next week. Ms. Aquino had posted a dozen claims. One of them read: All swans are white.

"Easy," said Tessa, who was already writing. "There are swans at the pond. We count them, they're all white, we win."

"Counting them doesn't win it," Alex said. He'd stood at that pond for twenty minutes last Saturday. Eleven swans, every one white. "If we see a hundred white swans, does that prove the claim?"

Ivy looked up from her sheet. "Prove all swans everywhere are white? From this one pond?"

"So what does break it?" Tessa said.

Alex thought about the word on the board under the title: hypothesis. A guess you could test. A test could support it or knock it down, and those were different jobs. "Seeing white swans supports it," he said slowly. "But it can't prove it. Not a hundred of them. Not a million." He tapped the pond claim. "But if we see one black swan, just one, the whole thing falls apart."

"Then we go find a black swan," Ivy said.

The pond gave them nothing but white. Tessa wanted to move to the optics hall, but Alex kept his eyes on the water, and on the reed bed near the fence, where something dark moved that wasn't a shadow. It glided out between two white swans, black as wet slate, and began pulling pondweed.

"Unanimous?" Ivy said, holding up her phone. "We all agree that's a swan?"

"That's a swan," Alex said. "That's a black swan."

Tessa wrote it down, and her hand was shaking slightly, which she covered by pointing at the bird as if it might need identifying twice.

They ran the sheet up to Ms. Aquino at the front desk. She read it, looked over their heads toward the pond, and pulled out the passes. "The black swan arrived last month from another centre," she said. "The old bird keeper retired the same week, and he never updated the claim board. Nice testing."

"Alex figured out the counting part," Tessa said.

"Figured it out standing right there," Alex said, pointing back at the reeds.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many U.S. schools require a sports physical, a checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before a student is allowed to try out or practice with a team.
story:
Sophie had the tryout schedule taped to her bedroom door, three days of basketball drills starting Monday, and she had practiced her crossover in the driveway every evening that week. On Saturday morning she dug through her backpack for the permission slip her mother had signed, planning to fold it into her gym bag where she couldn't lose it. Under the math homework she found a folded note instead, written on loose-leaf in Arwen's round, careful handwriting.

"Sophie. Bring your physical form on Monday. Mr. Ho won't let anyone try out without it. My brother learned that the hard way last year. Call me."

Sophie read it twice, then sat down on the edge of her bed. Permission slip, yes. Emergency contact card, yes. Physical form, she had never heard of it. She tried to picture Monday: the gym, the cones, Mr. Ho at the door with his clipboard. What would he actually check for? The permission slip got you into the building, probably, but Arwen's note made it sound like something else stood between a player and the court. She despised not knowing the rules before a game, and this felt like a game she hadn't been told about.

She made an inference from the word itself. A physical had to involve a body, so it was probably about being healthy enough to play. She could guess that. What she couldn't see was who counted, a doctor only, or someone else, and what would happen at the door if the paper wasn't signed. Arwen's brother had found out the hard way, which meant he had shown up and been turned away. Sophie pulled on the elastic band around her wrist, snapped it once, and went to find her mother in the kitchen.

"It's a checkup by a doctor," her mother said, looking up from the grocery list. "Or another clinician, like the nurse practitioner at the clinic on Miller Street. A lot of schools here require it before a student can try out or practice with a team. Yours does." She turned over an envelope on the counter. "This came home in your folder two weeks ago. It's the form."

Sophie took the envelope. Inside was a single page with blanks for height, weight, and a signature line at the bottom. The clinic on Miller Street took walk-ins on Saturdays, her mother said, but it was already eleven, and the appointment could take an hour if there was a wait.

"Can we go now?" Sophie asked.

"We can try."

They drove with the windows cracked, the form flat on Sophie's lap under her hand so it wouldn't slide. In the waiting room she texted Arwen: going to clinic, tell Mr. Ho I might be late Monday. The receptionist clicked her keyboard, then said the nurse practitioner could see her at noon. Sophie sat between her mother and a man reading a fishing magazine, and when the door at the end of the hall opened and a voice called her name, she stood up, form in hand, and walked toward it.

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: The side that proposes a change carries the burden of proof, meaning it must show why the change is needed rather than the other side proving it is not.
story:
Camille spread her debate notes across the living room carpet, and Aarya dropped a stack of index cards on top of them like a collapsing tower. "Faisal's coming in twenty minutes," Aarya said, "and we still don't have a case. The tournament is tomorrow."

The topic was printed at the top of Camille's paper: the school should switch to a four-day week. Faisal burst through the door with a granola bar in his mouth and said, around it, "Easy. We just say the four-day week is great, and the other team has to prove it isn't."

Camille frowned at her cards. Something about that felt wobbly, like a stool missing a leg. She tried to picture the judge, a tired-looking adult with a clipboard, listening to them say "it's great" and nothing else. The other team would just shrug. "Wait," she said. "If we're the ones who want to change the rule, maybe we're the ones who have to show it's needed."

"Burden of proof," Faisal said, licking granola off his thumb. "My cousin debates. The side that proposes a change carries the burden of proof. That means it has to show why the change is needed, instead of the other side proving it's not."

"So if we stand up there and say nothing, we lose even if they say nothing too," Camille said. "That's like being accused of eating the last cookie and having to prove you didn't." Aarya pointed at her. "You always eat the last cookie. That's a different kind of proof."

They rebuilt the case on the carpet. "Claim," Camille said, writing the word on a fresh card. "Four-day weeks save money on buses. Evidence: the district transportation budget is public, and running buses one fewer day cuts costs." Aarya squinted at it. "Okay, but why does cheaper buses mean we should do it? What's the link?"

"That's the warrant," Faisal said, waving his granola bar like a pointer. "You connect the evidence to the claim." Camille chewed her pencil. The budget number by itself didn't symbolize anything to a judge; it was just ink on a card until they explained what it meant. She wrote: if the school saves money on buses, it can spend that money on other things, so the change is worth making. "There," she said. "Claim, evidence, warrant. One card per point. Three points. Analysis, not just yelling."

Aarya held up a card shaped like a lopsided star. "My warrant is that tired students like me symbolize the failure of the five-day week." Camille snatched it. "No symbolizing yourself, Aarya." Faisal collapsed sideways onto the couch, laughing, then sat up fast. "What's the most probable thing the other team will say? Families need somewhere for kids on the fifth day."

Camille flipped the card over and wrote their answer underneath. Then she lined up all the cards in order on the coffee table, squared the edges, and dealt them out like a winning hand. "Sixty seconds to practice," she said, and tapped the timer on her phone.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The rule of thirds is a composition guideline that divides a picture into a three-by-three grid and places the main subject along those lines or where they cross.
story:
Norah had drawn the heron eleven times, and every version bored her. She sat at the long table by the window of the community art studio, her sketchbook open to a page where the bird stood dead center, gray and stiff, like something preserved in a museum drawer.

"It's accurate," said Cecily, leaning over from the next stool. "It just doesn't do anything."

"I know." Norah flipped back through the earlier tries. Same pose, same placement. Last summer she had entered a drawing of her grandmother's cottage in the county fair, putting the cottage right in the middle of the paper, and it hadn't even placed. At the time she blamed the judge. Now she wondered if the problem had been hers all along, sitting quietly in the middle of everything she made.

Ms. Gallagher was helping a younger kid at the clay table, but Norah had heard her say something to another student a few weeks ago, something about not parking your subject in the center like a car in a garage. Norah hadn't listened properly. She remembered only fragments: thirds, lines, crossing points. Maybe there was an actual rule, some pattern she couldn't see directly, hidden in pictures that worked.

She turned to a fresh page and drew a quick three-by-three grid, nine equal boxes. Then she sketched the heron again, but this time she placed its eye at one of the spots where two grid lines crossed, off to the left, and let the reeds run along the bottom horizontal line. The bird seemed to lean into the empty space beside it, as if it might lift off the page.

"Whoa," Cecily said. "It moves."

Norah held the old drawing beside the new one. Same heron, same reeds, and yet one sat there while the other lived. The rule of thirds, she thought, that was probably what Ms. Gallagher had called it. She tested it against the old cottage drawing in her memory, imagining a grid over it, and winced; the cottage had been planted exactly in the center box like a stamp on an envelope. It almost embarrassed her, all those years of parking everything in the middle.

"Try your parliament of owls," Cecily said, pointing at Norah's folder of reference photos, a whole flock of them crowded on a fence in the tranquil blue light of dusk. Norah laid a loose grid over the photo with her pencil, moved the fence line to the lower third, the biggest owl onto a crossing point, and began to draw.

Behind them, the studio door opened and Ms. Gallagher called out, "Norah, five minutes to cleanup."

"Can I have ten?" Norah said, already shading the owl's eye.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person often also chants the haftarah, a reading from the books of the Prophets.
story:
"Grandma, I've got the Torah portion mostly memorized," Claire announced, dropping her notebook on the kitchen table. "Eleven verses. I can chant eight of them without looking." Grandma slid a plate of mandel bread toward her and pulled out the opposite chair. Outside the window, a line of migratory geese crossed the gray sky, and Claire watched them for a second before getting back to business. Her bat mitzvah was in three months, and she wanted to be the most prepared student her tutor had ever seen.

Grandda turned from the stove, stirring his soup. "Good, good. And the other one?"

"The other what?"

"The other reading." He said it the way he said everything, mild and unhurried, like he'd asked whether she wanted honey in her tea.

Claire flipped through her notebook. There was only one portion in there, one set of taped tropp notes, one recording she played on the bus. "Grandda, I only have one."

He raised an eyebrow at Grandma, who shrugged and said, "You'd better call your tutor, bubbele."

Claire ran upstairs, phone in hand, and called her friend Alys, whose brother had been bar mitzvahed two years ago. Alys picked up on the first ring. "Okay, so at a bar or bat mitzvah you also chant the haftarah," Alys said immediately, "which is a reading from the books of the Prophets. Eli had to do both. He complained about it for a solid month."

Claire sat down hard on the guest bed. Two readings. Not one. She had been so proud of her eight verses, and now the whole mountain had doubled in height. "How long is a haftarah?" she asked, already pulling a fresh page toward her.

"Long enough. Eli's was maybe twenty-something verses."

After dinner, Claire spread her notes across the kitchen table and made a plan. Monday through Thursday, she'd revise the Torah portion in the mornings before school, because her voice was sharper then, and tackle the haftarah in the evenings when Grandda could listen. He didn't chant anymore, he said, but his ears still worked fine. She drew a calendar on the back of an envelope, three months of boxes, and colored the Shabbat before her ceremony gold.

"Look at this," she said, turning the envelope toward him. "Eight weeks to haftarah, three weeks of overlap, then polish. My tutor thinks I'm a maniac, by the way. He called me an overachiever."

"He means it as praise," Grandda said, tapping the gold box with his spoon. "Now chant me those eight verses. From the top."

Claire stood, squared her shoulders, and began.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.
story:
Joseph's father handed him a folded newspaper page in the hospital family room and said, "They'll run it tomorrow." Joseph unfolded it slowly, because he already knew what it was. He had seen one last year when his friend Frederique's aunt died, and Frederique had explained it to him then: an obituary, a published notice of someone's death, usually with a short account of their life, like their family, their work, their interests. This one was his grandfather's.

The room was quiet except for a vending machine humming against the wall. Nizar sat beside Joseph with his coat still on, because he had come straight from school when he heard. Joseph read the first lines, which listed who Grandpa belonged to, and his eyes caught on a sentence in the middle. Before he retired, he served as a sailor on freight ships crossing the Atlantic. Joseph read it twice. "He never told me that," he said. "Eight years, Nizar. He talked about tomatoes and card games. Never once the ocean."

Nizar leaned over to look. "Maybe it's a mistake," he said. Joseph thought about that. The facts in an obituary were supposed to be true, gathered by the family, so if it was a mistake, somebody had made it. His father was still across the room talking to Mr. Kowalski, the neighbour who had driven them here, so Joseph went and asked him directly. "Dad. The sailor part. Is that real?"

His father rubbed his eyes. "Fourteen years old, he signed on. He quit when your mom was born. He didn't like remembering it, I think, but it's real." A strange, small idea began to germinate in Joseph's head: there had been a whole other grandfather, one who had climbed ropes in storms, and Joseph had never asked a single question about him. He had figured he knew the man completely, and he had been wrong.

"I never even asked," Joseph said to Nizar when he sat back down. Nizar shrugged, not unkindly. "You were optimistic about it," he said. "You thought you had time." Joseph looked at the newspaper page again, at the symmetry of it, how the small square notice held an entire life in even little rows, and how little of it he had actually seen while the man was alive.

Mr. Kowalski stood and stretched. "I'm going to get coffee before the drive home," he said. "Anyone coming?" Joseph folded the page carefully and put it in his jacket pocket, where it would not crease, and stood up.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
story:
Evan stood in the pharmacy line at Mapleview Mall with twenty dollars in his pocket and his little sister's allergy pills in his sights. He had walked here after school because their mom was working late, and the pill bottle at home was down to two tablets. The line snaked past a rack of sunglasses, and somewhere behind him a baby fussed and a woman comforted it in a low, patient voice.

The price on the shelf tag made him stop and reread it. Twelve dollars last month, sixteen now. He counted the people ahead of him: nine, all holding the same blue box, plus a woman with a whole basket of them. When he finally reached the counter, the cashier rang him up without a pause, as if sixteen dollars were nothing unusual.

"Does anyone ever not buy them?" Evan asked, handing over his crumpled bills. "Because of the price?"

The cashier smiled tiredly. "Same line every day, same boxes. When the pollen season gets bad, they'd pay almost anything." She slid the box across the counter. "My economics teacher in high school called that inelastic demand."

Evan found Manuel and Bryson by the fountain, where they were supposed to be hunting for a birthday gift for their friend. Bryson was examining a rack of keychains that had been eight dollars before the new game came out and were now three dollars each, in a pile nobody touched. "Nobody wants these anymore," Bryson said. "They can't even give them away."

Evan sat down between them and turned the pharmacy box over in his hands. "So when everybody wants something and there isn't much of it, the price climbs," he said slowly, "and when there's tons of something nobody wants, the price drops. But my sister's pills went up four dollars and the line was out the door anyway."

"Because people need them," Manuel said. "Nobody needs a keychain."

Evan wanted to make sure he had it right, so he tested it. At the snack cart he asked the vendor which drink sold out fastest on rainy days. "Hot chai, always," the vendor said. "When the monsoon rains come, everyone wants something warm. I run out, so the price goes up a little. In summer I can't sell it at all, so it goes down." Evan nodded. The hot drink, like the pills, was something people kept buying no matter the price. The keychains, like iced chai in a downpour, could be cheap and still sit there.

On the bus home, Evan held the pill box on his lap and watched the mall shrink in the window, its prices volatile as weather, some things soaring, some falling, while the little blue box stayed steady in his hands. At his stop he hurried through the drizzle, and when his sister met him at the door he shook the box beside his ear, rattling it. "Enough to last the whole season," he said.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Scoring a line on thick card with a blunt tool before folding it gives a straight, clean fold instead of a cracked, bumpy one.
story:
Jordan had promised his grandmother a handmade card for her birthday, and the third attempt lay cracked open on the library table like something that had been dropped. The fold ran crooked and bumpy, the card stock split along a jagged white line, and his ink drawing of her old kitchen was ruined. He had two sheets of thick card left. Ms. Ramírez had set out a donation box of craft supplies at the front desk, paper the library had gotten when a stationery shop closed, and once it was gone there would be no more.

Across the table, Hank was building a model bridge out of coffee stirrers for the heritage fair, since his topic was an old covered bridge in his grandfather's town. He wanted the model to hold a full can of soda, and so far it held a paperback and nothing else.

"Fold it slower," Hank said, without looking up.

"I did fold it slower. Look at it." Jordan held up the ruined card. "The first two cracked too, and I scored nothing, I creased nothing, I just folded."

He sat back and thought about the paper itself. He could not see inside the card, but every fold cracked in the same way, so something about the thick card had to be the same each time. Thin paper folded fine at home yesterday. The difference was the thickness. Maybe thick card could not take a sharp fold all at once, and the crack was the paper giving up along the fold line.

He remembered something in the donation box, a plastic thing that looked like a dull knife. Blunt, not sharp. An impulsive kid would have ignored it, but he went and got it. He laid a ruler along where he wanted the fold, drew the blunt tool down the line once, pressing hard, and felt the card give a faint tick. Then he folded it.

The fold came out straight and clean. No crack, no bump. The scored side looked like a hinge.

"Blunt tool, ruler, one firm line before you fold," Jordan said, laying the folded card flat.

Hank put down his stirrers and came around the table. He took the plastic tool and a spare piece of card, scored a line down the middle of it, folded it, and turned it over to check.

"Every stirrer wall I make cracks when I bend it for the arch," Hank said. He was already stacking stirrers side by side and scoring the top of the row. Ms. Ramírez came by with the donation box and paused over the clean folds spread across the table.

"Making cards?" she asked.

"Making hinges," Jordan said, and scored another line.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
story:
Tyler had a history assignment due Friday: pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in his own words. The trouble was that he did not understand the thing at all. He spread the photocopies across the library table under the humming fluorescent light, smelling the old-paper scent of the room, and glared at the pages as if they might blink first.

"You look like you're about to feed that to the shredder," said Aliyah, sliding into the chair across from him with her own stack of books. Atticus followed, dropping his backpack with a thud that made the librarian frown.

"It's broken," Tyler said. "Look. Section 2 says everyone has freedom of expression. Great. But then section 1 says the rights are guaranteed only subject to reasonable limits. What does that even mean? It's like selling someone a bike and then saying, except you can't ride it."

Atticus leaned over the page, and his finger traced the sentence. "It says the limits have to be reasonable and, wait, keep reading. Subject to reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. That's the whole thing. Section 1 of the Charter actually says that."

Aliyah tapped the table. "So the right is real, but it has a border around it. Like a soccer field. You can play anywhere on the grass, but not out of bounds."

Tyler sat back. He had assumed the assignment was asking him to memorize a list, but maybe it was asking something sneakier: how the border worked. He decided to test it. "Okay, Atticus. Say I stand on a bench outside school and shout that your shoes are terrible."

"Rude," said Atticus, "but probably allowed."

"Now say I shout it during your solo in the choir concert, on purpose, so nobody can hear you."

Atticus winced. "That would be the worst night of my life."

"So that's it," Tyler said, and the feeling of it landing was like a gear finally catching. "The limit has to be justified. Stopping me at the concert protects your performance, so it's reasonable. Stopping me on the bench protects nothing." He pulled a fresh sheet toward him and began writing, his pen accelerating across the page, sentences coming faster than he could print them.

Mr. Gauthier, the librarian, paused at their table on his rounds. "Someone's defiant about homework," he said, nodding at Tyler's hunched shoulders.

"Not defiant, just busy," Tyler said. "Thanks, though." He slid his half-finished paragraph across to Aliyah. "Read this and tell me if it makes sense. I'll buy you a juice box at the corner store as the expense of my allowance, but I'm not rewriting it more than twice."

"Deal," said Aliyah, and began to read.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah, making the trip west far faster than by wagon.
story:
Mila had promised Ms. Somsak a primary source by Monday, and all she had was a photocopied page of a settler's diary from 1868, folded into her jacket pocket, and Angel, who was late. She stood at the war memorial with its long wall of names, waiting, reading the diary again. The settler, a woman named only H., wrote about her brother who had gone ahead to California and the two children she had buried on the trail. Mila underlined one line: "We go because staying is also a kind of dying." It sounded important, but she couldn't yet say what it proved.

"Sorry," Angel panted, skidding up on his bike. "I had to drop my brother at the railway museum. He works there now. Come on, you can copy stuff there." Mila followed him the three blocks, diary still in hand. Inside, past a model of a steam engine, Angel's brother was leading a school group, and Mila drifted close enough to listen.

"So imagine your family in a wagon," he was saying. "Months on the trail. Now look at this date." He pointed at a photograph of men shaking hands over a rail line. "The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah. After that, the trip west took days by train instead of months by wagon."

The kids murmured, but Mila felt something click. Here was the paradox she'd been circling all week: the diary said the trail killed children, yet families kept going. If the crossing itself was the danger, then after May 10, 1869, the danger shrank and more people could choose to go. The diary couldn't explain the crowds; the railroad could. The hidden cause wasn't courage. It was the train. She pulled out her notebook and wrote fast, testing the idea against the page: H.'s family left in 1868, one year too early, the last dangerous year.

"Is that real or counterfeit?" Angel asked, squinting at the photograph, the kind of question that could provoke his brother into a lecture, which it did, fifteen minutes about reenactments and originals. Mila only half listened. When they left, the sky had gone gray and her mother had texted twice, so Saturday was gone, and she'd missed the movie she'd wanted. She walked Angel to the corner with her notebook under her arm.

On Monday Ms. Somsak read the essay twice, then set it down. "This is what I asked for," she said. "The diary tells you why one family went. The railroad tells you why thousands did. You used both." Mila smiled, then thought of H. writing by candlelight, one year too early, never knowing that the thing which would have saved her children was already being hammered into place somewhere in the mountains.

"Do I get an A?" Mila asked.

Ms. Somsak handed the page back, and on it, in red, was one word: "Revise."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
story:
The poster hung outside the art room, black and white, and Jace had walked past it three times before Ronin stopped dead in front of it and said, "That's a weird picture of a vase."

"A vase?" Jace stared at it. All he could see were two faces, nose to nose, like a photo of twins about to bump foreheads. "It's two faces. Look, there's a chin. There's another chin."

"There's no chin." Ronin traced the air with his finger. "See the curvy sides? That's the vase."

Kaylee came down the hall with her backpack over one shoulder. "Whose chin? What are you two arguing about now?"

"The poster," Jace said. "It's two faces."

She stopped, squinted. "It's obviously a vase."

"You too?" Jace leaned closer until his nose almost touched the paper. Faces, definitely faces. The foreheads, the little dip where the mouths would be. How could Ronin and Kaylee be looking at the same ink and seeing something completely different? Maybe one of them was messing with him. He decided to test it. "Okay, Kaylee. Close your eyes. Now open them and tell me the first thing you see, fast, don't think."

She opened her eyes. "Vase."

"Ronin?"

"Vase," Ronin said. "Told you."

Jace looked again, determined to force a vase out of it. If the white part in the middle was a vase, then the black on either side would have to be the background. He tried to make the black shrink backward in his mind, the way camouflage disappears into the background, and for a second the white bulged forward like a real pot sitting on a table. Then it snapped back into two faces again, and the vase was gone, like a word he couldn't hold onto.

Mr. Thompson came out of the art room carrying a box of brushes. "You've discovered the Rubin vase," he said, setting the box down.

"The what?"

"Rubin vase. Edgar Rubin, 1915." He tapped the poster. "You can see it as a vase or as two faces, but never both at the same time."

"Never both," Jace repeated. That was the part that got him. Not that people disagreed, but that his own eyes wouldn't let him hold both pictures at once.

"It's like that argument you two had last week," Kaylee said slowly. "About whether the new cafeteria rule was fair. You both saw the same rule."

Ronin made a face at her, then made a face at the poster. "Okay," he said. "But I still say the vase is better."

"That's because you like pottery," Jace said. "I'm going to see faces. But at least now I know why we're both right." He pulled out his phone and took a photo of the poster. "For the essay. I'm going to cite it."

Ronin peered at the picture on the screen. "Huh. In the photo it looks like faces."

"Give me that," Kaylee said, grabbing the phone, and waved it back and forth like it might shake loose an answer.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment.
story:
The moving truck pulled away at noon, and Ryder stood on a street where every mailbox had a number but no face behind it yet. In his old town, he'd have been at Moses's house by now, or dragging his skateboard to the lot behind Matthias's building. He resented the boxes stacked in the hallway, and he resented his father for stacking them so neatly, like this was all settled.

He took the skateboard out anyway. Halfway down the block, two boys were drawing a chalk course across a driveway, tight turns around a broom laid flat. "You get three runs," the taller one said, not looking up. "Best time wins."

"Wins what?"

"Naming rights on the course."

Ryder lost the first run by a full second and won the second by half of one. The boys were Matthias and Moses, which he found funny for about a minute and then stopped mentioning, because they weren't his Matthias and Moses, and saying the names out loud made that worse. He pushed hard through the third run, vigorous even on the flat, and took the course record. They wrote RYDER in chalk at the top of the driveway.

Back home, he found a folder on his bed that his mother must have gotten from the school. Inside was a photocopied page from a handout, and he read it twice at the kitchen table. On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools were listed as life events that require readjustment. He'd assumed the flat, heavy feeling was something wrong with him specifically, some defect he'd carried across state lines in his own head. It had a source. It had been measured by two people with names, in a year before his parents were even born.

He remembered the last day at his old school, when Moses had punched his arm at the bus loop and said, "Don't be a stranger," and Ryder had said "Yeah" while already thinking about the packing tape in the garage. He'd believed the move would hit once, on moving day, and then be over. It hadn't worked that way. The page didn't promise when it would end, only that readjustment took something out of you while it happened.

The next morning, Ms. Desir from next door was watering her mums, and she called across the fence, "You're the new boy. How's it going?"

"Moving and new school," Ryder said. "Readjustment."

She laughed. "Someone's been doing homework."

He picked up the skateboard. "Race you to the corner."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun also gets longer days, giving sunlight more hours to warm the ground.
story:
Asher had promised Ms. Rivera he could explain the seasons by Monday, and so far all he had was a sentence he'd copied from the board: the tilt of Earth's axis causes them. He knew the words but not the reason, and that felt like owing someone money.

At the kitchen table he set down an orange and a desk lamp. He had poked a chopstick through the orange to be the axis, though it went in crooked because the peel had negotiated with him the whole way, splitting where he pushed hardest. He marked a dot near the top with a marker and labeled it in his head: us.

First he tilted the chopstick toward the lamp and spun the orange slowly. The dot stayed in the light the whole turn, from the moment it rotated into view until it swung around the back, and even then it slid through the glow at the edge before going dark. "Wait," he said out loud. He tilted the chopstick away from the lamp and spun again. This time the dot spent half the spin in shadow, then only a thin slice of light before darkness again.

He pulled out his phone and checked something he'd noticed last July without thinking about it: at summer camp, his counselor had called lights-out at nine, and the sky outside had still been blue-gray. In December it was pitch black by five. He wrote "longer days in summer" beside his drawing of the orange.

Abby called at seven to ask what he was doing, and he told her about the crooked chopstick. "So the half tilted toward the Sun is the half having summer," she said, "and that's also the half with the longer days?" Asher looked at the orange, its top dot lit for almost the whole spin. "Yeah. More hours of sunlight hitting the ground, more time to warm it up." There was the insight, and it had come from a fruit and a lamp and a memory of a bedtime that came before dark.

He decided to bring the orange to class anyway. Ms. Rivera said demonstrations were welcome, so he would hold it up, tilt the chopstick toward the window, and say the same thing he'd told Abby. He put the orange in a plastic container, packed it on top of his notes, and carried the whole thing to the front door so he couldn't forget it in the morning.

"Hairbrush, charger, orange," he said, checking the bag one last time.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: A bond held until its maturity date pays back its full face value, as long as the issuer does not default, no matter how its price moved in between.
story:
The lemonade stand sat at the end of Cole's driveway, and behind it he had taped a sign that read "Ask me about stocks and bonds, 50 cents extra." Ms. Morin had assigned it two days ago: learn the difference, explain which is riskier and why, and be ready to present on Monday. Cole figured if he could explain it to strangers buying lemonade, he could explain it to anyone.

His first customer was Leslie, who rode up on her bike just as the afternoon heat sent every kid in the neighborhood migrating toward cold drinks. "What's the extra fifty cents get me?" she asked, counting quarters into the tin.

"A lecture," Cole admitted. "Ms. Morin's assignment. Stocks and bonds."

Leslie dropped in two more quarters and sat on the curb. Cole poured her a cup and started with what he'd worked out. "A stock is a tiny piece of a company, so its price goes wherever the company goes, up or down. A bond is different. You lend your money, and when the bond matures, you get the full face value back. That's what maturity means, the date it pays you back."

Leslie sipped her lemonade. "So which is riskier?"

Before he could answer, Zoey came running down the sidewalk, phone in her hand, her face pale. "Cole. My grandma gave me that bond for my birthday and I checked it today and the price dropped. It dropped. Did I lose money?"

Cole felt his own stomach tighten, remembering how he'd panicked last month when the stock he'd bought with birthday money fell four dollars and he'd sold it in a rush at a loss. He still wondered whether he should have waited. "When does it mature?" he asked.

Zoey stared at the screen. "It says 2041."

"Then look," Cole said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "A bond held until its maturity date pays back its full face value, as long as the issuer doesn't default, no matter how its price moved in between. The price can dip all it wants. If you hold it to 2041, you still get the whole face value back."

"Default?" Zoey asked.

"That's when the issuer can't pay. It doesn't happen much, but it can."

Zoey lowered the phone. Her shoulders came down from around her ears. "So I don't actually lose anything unless that happens, or unless I sell it now like an idiot."

"Like I did with my stock," Cole said. He hadn't meant to say it out loud. Leslie laughed, not unkindly, and he laughed too, a little.

"So the stock is riskier," Leslie said. "Its price is real the whole time. The bond's dip is just noise."

Cole frowned. He thought about inflation, which could quietly eat the value of that payoff by 2041, and about his uncle, who always said the birds that winter here instead of flying migratory routes take their chances too. Maybe risk wasn't one thing with one answer. He reached for the marker and changed the sign.

"Ask me about stocks and bonds. The answer costs a dollar now."

Leslie groaned and dug in her pocket.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story The Monkey's Paw, Sergeant-Major Morris warns that the paw's wishes bring terrible results and throws it into the fire before the family rescues it.
story:
The porch swing at Grandma's house had one stable leg and one that wobbled, so Ruby learned to calibrate her weight, sitting slightly left, before she spread out her notebook and the photocopy of "The Monkey's Paw." English was on Monday, and Ms. Pierre had promised the essay question would be about foreshadowing and symbolism, and Ruby had promised herself she would not write "the paw is just a paw."

Her phone buzzed against her knee. Parker.

stuck on question 2. why does morris throw the paw in the fire?? i wrote "because it is on fire" lol

Ruby laughed, then stopped. Actually, that moment was strange. She read the page again, and there it was: the sergeant-major holding the dried little paw over the flames, and Mr. White diving to snatch it out. Morris didn't drop it by accident. He threw it. She flipped back to the earlier page, hunting for what he'd said, and found that too. He had flat out warned them. The wishes came true, he said, but so badly, so terribly, that he'd rather burn the thing than let it keep ruining people.

parker she typed. he warned them BEFORE the first wish. the whole story warns them.

That was it. That was foreshadowing, not just a vocabulary word. The fire, the chess game Mr. White kept losing, the cold wind. If she could show that the warning came first and the family ignored it anyway, she had an essay.

Inside, Grandma was at the kitchen table sorting boxes, because the house was being sold in the spring and every shelf had to be emptied before then. "Did you find your answer?" she called through the screen door.

"I think so. The soldier told them the wishes were terrible and tried to burn the paw, and they took it anyway."

Grandma set down a stack of Grandpa's old records. "People do that. Take the thing they were warned about." She said it lightly, but the boxes said the rest.

Ruby looked at her essay outline, then at the swing where Grandpa used to sit and insist the story was really about greed, which she now suspected was not quite right either. She added a line to her notes: maybe the paw is a symbol for wanting more than what you have, and the fire is what happens to people who don't let go of it. That felt true and a little too neat at the same time.

Parker texted again.

ok but WHY do the wishes go wrong?? the story never says

Ruby stared at the question. He was right, it never did. The warnings were all they got, and maybe that was the point, that you had to judge from warnings alone. She started typing, then put the phone face down on the porch boards and picked up her pen instead.

The wind chime on the eaves rang once, and she underlined the fire scene twice.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Arthur kept folding the corner of his appointment slip until it went brittle and cracked off in his fingers. He was here because for three months his stomach had cramped every morning before school, and last Tuesday he had walked out of a math quiz halfway through because his hands would not stop shaking. His mom had finally stopped saying "just eat breakfast" and made the appointment, though she had to leave the car running outside, which meant Arthur had exactly forty minutes to figure out what to say.

He was not alone in the row of chairs. Mayar from his art class sat two seats down, turning her phone over and over in her lap like she was hoping a message would appear on the back of it. Her younger brother had an appointment, she said, and her mom had asked her to come along to help carry his things. She kept checking the clock.

"You look like I feel," Arthur said.

She laughed, but it came out thin. "I used to look worse. I used to be here for me, like every month." She held up her phone, which showed a photo of a therapy dog with a crooked bandana. "That's Jelly. My coping plan has Jelly in it, and running, and saying no to stuff." She glanced toward the front desk. "The saying no part is boundaries. My coach wanted me at five practices a week and I wanted to sleep."

Arthur frowned. His stomach had been fine all summer at his grandmother's house, and it only started when school began. That was a pattern. It was not food, because food did not know what day it was. "So what was actually wrong with you?" he asked.

"Anxiety disorder," Mayar said, like she was naming a town she used to live in. "Everyone feels anxious sometimes, that part's normal. Mine just got so loud it lasted for months and got in the way of everything, so a doctor diagnosed me. It's treatable. It got better after I told a doctor about it, the actual true stuff, not the fine-I'm-fine stuff."

Arthur thought about that. Loud, long, in the way. His stomach was not exactly in the way, but it did obstruct things, quietly, like a chair pushed into a doorway. And he had not slept properly since September; the fatigue showed in the mirror some mornings, gray under his eyes.

When the nurse called his name, he stood up and his legs felt strange, but he followed her down the hall. Ms. Fernando listened to his stomach story all the way through without interrupting, and she asked what he did on mornings when it was worst.

"I make tea," Arthur said. "It doesn't really work."

"That's a coping attempt," she said, writing something down. "We can build better ones. But first tell me the true stuff, not the fine-I'm-fine stuff."

He almost said he was fine. Instead he said, "I walked out of a quiz. I left my friend Clarke sitting there alone. I think something's been running the whole show since September and I don't know what it is."

Ms. Fernando set down her pen. "That's a good place to start."

Back in the waiting room afterward, with a referral card in his pocket and a follow-up appointment that meant missing part of art class, Arthur found Mayar still there, still turning her phone over. Her brother had been taken in without her.

"He wouldn't let me come with him," she said. "Says I hover. New boundary, apparently. Mine, not his." She managed half a smile. "How was the true stuff?"

"Harder than the tea," Arthur said, and handed her the brittle corner of his appointment slip, folded into a tiny paper boat.

She set it on the magazine table between them. "For the next person who's scared," she said.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street, so the fronts of objects face you and everything else recedes to one point.
story:
Emmett stood in front of a painting of a narrow street, his sketchbook open, his pencil hovering. The gallery was quiet except for the hum of the air vents, and Makenzie had wandered off toward the watercolors, leaving him alone with the picture. He had been trying to draw streets all week, and every one of them came out wrong, the buildings leaning like they might slide off the page. Mr. Nielsen, his art teacher, had said something once about lines meeting at a single point, but Emmett had half-listened, and now that lesson seemed to have evaporated out of his head entirely.

He found the point in the painting almost by accident. Every roofline, every curb, every row of bricks ran toward one spot between two buildings near the middle. He marked it in his sketchbook with a small x and started drawing his own street, letting every edge run toward the x like water finding a drain. It actually worked. The buildings stood up straight for the first time, and the street pulled the eye down its middle.

On Saturday he tried it again outside, standing at the corner of Maple and Third with Coen, who was eating sunflower seeds and watching him fail. Emmett drew his x, drew his lines, and the street still came out crooked, the buildings twisted as if the whole block were melting. "You said this worked," Coen said, spitting a shell into the gutter. "It worked at the gallery."

Emmett looked down the page, then down the actual street. At the gallery, the painter had stood in the middle of the road, straight on, so the fronts of the buildings faced the viewer like flat cards. Here at the corner, Emmett was looking down Maple, but the building right beside him turned its side face toward him, a whole second surface the flat-card drawing had never needed. He tested it, quick and dirty: he stepped off the curb into the middle of Maple, planted himself facing straight down the street, and drew again. Now every line obeyed the single x. "Get out of the road before you become a drawing," Coen called, but he came over to look.

"So you have to be straight-on," Emmett said. "One point works when you're facing straight down a street, and everything else goes back to that one spot."

"Then what do you do at a corner?"

Emmett stared at the side face of the brick building, the one that refused to cooperate, and wondered whether Mr. Nielsen had mentioned a second point somewhere in that lost lesson. He turned a fresh page and marked two x's instead of one.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land.
story:
Carson slid the glass case key across the table toward Mr. Lombardi, who unlocked the archive room at the old trail museum and pointed to a wooden box marked 1846.

"Forty minutes until the bus leaves," Will whispered, checking his phone for the third time. "We still need a topic for Monday's history project."

Ashley was already photographing land deeds, but Carson had a different problem. Their assignment asked them to use a primary source, an actual document from the time, to explain why so many families risked the dangerous trail west in the 1800s. He knew pioneers went. He did not know why anyone would leave a home for a two-thousand-mile walk into uncertainty.

He lifted a diary from the box, its leather cover cracked, its pages stained at the corners. The handwriting was cramped and faded, but he could make out the entries. The first ones, from spring, depicted a tidy farm in Ohio, with descriptions of new fences and a good wheat field. Then the tone changed. "The bank has taken the farm," one October entry read. "We have nothing left here. We will go west where the land is cheap and the soil is rich, and we will start again."

Carson read the line twice. He flipped forward, looking for the same pattern, testing a guess: if money trouble pushed this family out, maybe it pushed others too. The next folder held letters from a family in New York. "Ruined by the hard times," one letter said. "We hear Oregon soil is vigorous and the claims are nearly free." A third document, a farmer's account book from 1841, showed debts piling up month after month until the page went blank.

"That's weird," Carson said. "All of them lost everything around the same years."

Ashley leaned over, squinting at the diary. "My grandpa mentioned something about that once. The Panic of 1837. He said it caused a long economic depression in the United States."

"Depression, like people being sad?" Will asked.

"Like the whole country being broke," Ashley said. "For years."

Carson pulled his notebook over and wrote it down. The Panic of 1837 had ruined farmers all over, and the ruined ones went west, chasing cheap, fertile land. That was the answer to his question. These families had not wanted adventure. They had lost everything and were choosing a dangerous trail over no future at all. The diary's last entry made his chest tighten: "We lock the door tomorrow. Johnny is scared of the river crossings. I tell him the crossing we cannot survive is staying here with nothing."

"Ten minutes," Mr. Lombardi called from the doorway. He glanced at Carson's notes and nodded once, but said nothing, which Carson understood to mean he was on the right track.

"We can build the whole project around this," Carson said, photographing the diary pages with steady hands. "One family, one diary, one real reason."

On the bus, Carson gave Will the extra granola bar from his backpack, because Will always forgot lunch, and started drafting his first line: "In 1846, a farmer in Ohio wrote one sentence that explains a thousand wagons."

"Fifteen hundred words by Monday," Will said.

"Then I'd better keep writing," Carson said, and his pencil touched the page.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
story:
The bus rattled over the pothole by the gym, and Eva flattened her book club worksheet against her binder before it slid off her knees. Kyson leaned over the seat in front of her, holding his copy of "The Lighthouse Keeper" open to page eleven, where the keeper's lantern flickered twice before the storm.

"See? That's foreshadowing," Kyson said. "The lantern goes out, so the boat's going to crash at the end. Adaline agrees with me." Behind him, Adaline nodded and pointed at her own page, where she had underlined the same two sentences in green pen.

Eva read the passage again. "But the boat doesn't crash," she said. "We read the ending yesterday. The keeper finds the boat's log in his own cellar. The lantern doesn't have anything to do with it."

"Then why would the author put it in?" Kyson asked. He was quiet for a moment, then flipped to the back cover. "Everything in a story means something. That's what the poster in Mr. Brown's room says."

Eva looked out the window at the power lines that ran perpendicular to the road, dipping and rising with the poles. Somewhere down the line, she thought, there was voltage running through those wires, something you couldn't see but knew was there because of what it did. Maybe clues in stories worked the same way. She turned back to Kyson. "What if it's a trick? What if the author put the lantern in to make us expect a crash, so we'd be surprised when we're wrong?"

Adaline frowned. "Authors do that?" The bus lurched around a corner, and she grabbed the seat. "That seems like cheating."

"Maybe there's a word for it," Eva said. She scrolled through the class vocabulary list on her phone, thumb moving fast. Halfway down, under the terms for their short story unit, she found it. "Red herring. It says a red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion." She held the screen up between the seats. "So not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing."

Kyson took the phone and read it twice. "Then the flickering lantern is a red herring," he said slowly. "The author wanted us looking at the water instead of the cellar." He pulled out a red pen and crossed out his notes, then started a new page. "Okay. New theory. But you have to cooperate with me on the write-up, because Mr. Brown is going to ask us how we know the difference."

Adaline passed her green pen forward. "Underline the cellar description," she said. "Page twenty-four. It was there all along."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The simple interest formula is I = P x r x t: interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years.
story:
The flyer on the grocery store corkboard said OPEN A FIRST SAVER ACCOUNT, 3 PERCENT INTEREST, and Anais stopped her cart so fast that a jar of salsa rocked in the child seat. "Three percent," she whispered. Her birthday money, forty dollars from her grandmother, had been sitting in a shoebox since June. She pulled the flyer off the board and held it like a winning ticket.

"Find the good cereal?" Ansh asked, steering his own cart up beside her. He was on a mission tonight: his mother wanted the invasive kind of mint for the garden, the one that spread everywhere if you let it, and he was supposed to locate it in the plant aisle before it sold out. But he glanced at the flyer too. "Three percent of forty dollars is what, a dollar twenty?"

"That's just one year," Anais said. She dug a pencil out of her jacket pocket, the stubby one she kept for crosswords, and flattened the flyer against the cereal boxes. "Grandma says the bank pays you every year you leave the money in. I want to know what it looks like after five." Five years felt enormous, like planning a trip to the moon, and her stomach did an excited flip.

In the produce section, Ms. He was squeezing avocados with great seriousness. Anais had helped her last summer when a raccoon tried to thwart her compost plans, climbing the fence night after night until Ms. He rigged a lid with a bungee cord. Ms. He had taught her that compost was full of microbes, tiny living things that turned apple cores into dirt, and she liked to say the dirt was where the real money was. "Anais," she said now, "you look like you're solving a crime."

"Kind of." Anais showed her the flyer and her pencil marks. "Ansh says one year is a dollar twenty. So I did principal times rate times time. Forty times point zero three times five." She wrote I = P x r x t on the edge of the flyer. "That's six dollars. Six dollars for doing nothing."

Ms. He laughed and put an avocado in her basket. "The bank calls that simple interest. Plain and steady." She held up a second flyer, one for a different account. "This one says compound. I never did figure out the difference." Anais snatched it before Ms. He finished the sentence.

"That's the one Grandma argued about with Uncle Ray at Thanksgiving," Ansh said. "Remember, you told me." Anais did remember, and the memory came back sharp: the long table, the pie, her grandmother tapping her water glass and saying compound interest earns interest on your interest, and Uncle Ray waving his fork and saying no bank gives you money on money. Nobody had settled it because the mashed potatoes arrived. Anais had been eleven and had not cared. Tonight she cared enormously.

She leaned over the frozen peas and worked it out, line by line, Ansh reading numbers aloud while Ms. He watched like a judge. One dollar twenty the first year, the same the second, the same the third, the fourth, the fifth. Six dollars, exactly what the formula said. Then she tried the compound way, adding each year's interest before multiplying the next year, and the total crept higher than six dollars. "It's more," she said, staring at her own numbers. "The compound one is more than the simple one. Grandma won."

By the dairy case, Anais had made a decision that felt as big as choosing a college. "I'm opening the account Monday," she announced. "The compound one. My money is going to sit there and grow for five whole years." Ansh held up a pot of the mint he'd finally found, roots dangling. "Then by the time we're eighteen, you'll be rich and I'll have a garden nobody can thwart." Anais laughed and folded the flyer into her pocket, right next to the pencil.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
Arthur kept a notebook in his backpack, and after every practice he wrote down two numbers: shots taken and shots made. At the start of the season he had gone 8 for 20, which the assistant coach had marked on the stats sheet as 40 percent. Now, at the third home game, he was waiting to see whether his new numbers would appear on the sheet Mr. Iyer pinned to the gym wall after every match.

Harmony found him standing in front of the sheet before the game started. "You check that thing every time," she said. "Nobody else even looks at it."

Arthur tapped the column of percentages with one finger. "Because it's one number for everything I did all season. Eight makes, twelve misses, twenty games, all folded into 40 percent. It's like the whole story got squashed flat." He had made 10 of his last 20 in practice, and he wanted that on the wall where everyone could see it. The coach had to authorize any change to the sheet, and Mr. Iyer had to be the one to write it, so Arthur had asked them both before warm-ups. They had said yes.

During the game Arthur played twelve minutes and took two shots, missing one and banking the other in off the glass. After the buzzer, George got to the stats sheet first and read out loud. "Arthur, up ten. Mr. Iyer wrote it right here. Ten."

"Ten what?" Arthur pushed through the small crowd of players. The sheet said 50 percent next to his name, and beside it, in Mr. Iyer's narrow handwriting, a note: "up 10." But the local sports page, which George's dad read aloud on the drive over, had said something different about the team's shooting this month, something Arthur could not get out of his head. He sat on the bleacher with his notebook open and wrote both numbers down.

"Here's the thing," he said to Harmony and George, turning the notebook so they could see. "I went from 40 percent to 50 percent. That's ten." He drew a line between the two numbers. "But ten out of forty is a quarter. Ten, and twenty-five, and it's the same change. Both stories were right."

George frowned at the page. "So the paper saying twenty-five and Mr. Iyer saying ten, that's the same thing?"

"That's the same thing," Arthur said. He tried it out against the game he had just watched, in his head, the way he checked a shot by watching where it hit the rim. One number counted the steps between the two totals, and the other counted how big the steps were compared with where he started. Both were true at once, which felt strange, like standing in two spots on the court at the same time. He wondered whether his conscience should have told him earlier that a single number on a sheet was never the whole story, since it left out every miss and every make it was built from.

Mr. Iyer came over with his marker and drew a small arrow next to Arthur's name, moving him up two places in the team rankings. "Fundamental thing about these sheets," he said, capping the marker. "One number, many games." Arthur copied the arrow into his notebook, right beside the ten and the twenty-five.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end.
story:
The bus home from Westbrook Middle School always smelled like rain and orange peels, and Kaylee had gotten used to saving the seat next to Helen. For three weeks now she hadn't. Helen sat four rows up with the field hockey girls, and Kaylee sat alone with her science folder on her lap, watching the town roll past the transparent windows while she pretended not to care.

Ms. Das had assigned them a project that morning: find a real study, summarize it, and present it together in pairs. Kaylee had flipped through the binder of articles at lunch and stopped on one line. "A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end." She read it twice. She and Helen had been inseparable in seventh grade. Then Kaylee joined robotics and Helen joined field hockey, and by October they were texting each other less every week.

She began to hypothesize. If the study was right, then the drift wasn't anyone's fault; it was a pattern, the way two animals that end up in different habitats slowly stop sharing an adaptation that once matched. That idea made her feel better and worse at the same time, so she decided to test it. The project needed a partner, and Ms. Das had said pairs could choose. On the bus, Kaylee stood up, walked four rows forward, and dropped into the empty seat beside Helen before she could talk herself out of it.

"Want to present that friendship study together?" she asked. "The one with the 573 kids."

Helen looked up from her phone. "The one from seventh grade? That's kind of about us, isn't it."
