"Kind of exactly about us." Kaylee turned the folder so Helen could see the page. "We ended up on different teams this year. Different everything."

"So we're the less alike ones." Helen said it flat, then frowned. "That's depressing."

"It doesn't have to be." Kaylee pointed at the margin where she'd written a question mark. "The study says friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end. It doesn't say it has to end. It just means we'd have to try to be alike somewhere new."

Helen was quiet while the bus hissed to a stop and two sixth graders clattered down the steps. Then she said, "I liked building that marshmallow tower in your garage last summer. Before robotics ate you."

"You liked that?"

"I literally asked to come back and you were always at practice." Helen pulled the folder closer and read the first paragraph herself. "Okay. New plan. We do the presentation, and we also build something. Something that has nothing to do with hockey or robots."

"Like what?"

"Dunno. A birdhouse. My dad has tools he never uses." Helen wrote her name on the folder cover, right next to Kaylee's, the way she used to in seventh grade.

The bus turned onto Kaylee's street, and the two of them stayed in the seat until the driver called out her stop. Kaylee gathered the folder, and Helen said, "Same seat tomorrow?"

"Same seat tomorrow." Kaylee stepped down onto the curb, and through the window she watched Helen hold up the folder, both their names visible, before the bus pulled away.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
The last crate of strawberries sat on Mr. Takahashi's table with a new sign taped to the front: seven dollars a basket. Ruby read it twice, because last week the same strawberries had been four dollars.

"Seven?" said Mahee, who was standing beside her with three dollars and a lot of opinions. "That's robbery."

Mr. Takahashi wiped his hands on his apron. "Frost took half the crop up the valley. Everyone who comes by wants what's left, so the price is higher today. Next month, when the fields are full again, it'll drop." He nodded toward the far end of his table, where a whole flat of zucchini sat unwanted. "Zucchini, on the other hand, you can have for a dollar. Nobody wants it. There is too much of it."

Ruby picked up a basket and studied the berries, small and red and fewer than usual. She thought about the water-diamond thing her father had told her last night, from a book called The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776. A man named Adam Smith had pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet water will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal. Ruby had argued about it at dinner. "Water keeps you alive," she had said. "A diamond just sits there." Her father had shrugged and gone back to his noodles.

"Okay, I have a theory," Ruby said now. "The price isn't about how useful a thing is. It's about how much of it there is and how many people want it. Water is everywhere, so it's cheap. Diamonds are rare, so they're expensive. Strawberries are rare this week, so seven dollars." She looked at Mahee. "Watch. I'm going to test it."

She marched to the honey stall, where the beekeeper was pouring samples into little paper cups. "Excuse me," Ruby said. "Is your honey expensive because it's useful, or because there isn't much of it?"

The beekeeper laughed. "Both, I suppose. But mostly the second. My hives didn't fill the frames this year. The bees used most of the honey to insulate the colony through the cold spring. Packed it around the brood like pink stuff in an attic. So I have less to sell, and more people want it, so the price went up."

Ruby wrote that down on the back of her hand with a pen from her backpack. Then she and Mahee walked the whole market, checking prices against pile sizes. The stall with one crate of peaches charged five dollars. The stall with four tables of bread charged two. The man selling handmade birdhouses had raised his price because a magazine had shown his work, and now forty people wanted one, though there were six birdhouses. That was legitimate, Mahee admitted, even if it was still too much money for a house meant for birds, who got theirs free.

"See, it's a rule," Ruby said. "Wanting plus not-enough governs the price. Wanting nothing plus piles of it makes zucchini." She counted her money: five dollars and some lint.

She went back to Mr. Takahashi's stall. "If I wait until closing," she asked, "will the price drop? The strawberries will be even scarcer tomorrow, but nobody here will want them tonight."

He scratched his chin. "You drive a hard bargain for someone wearing a cat backpack."

"It has good insulation. Keeps my water cold."

At six o'clock, when the lanterns came on and the crowd thinned to dog walkers, Mr. Takahashi called her over. "Five dollars," he said, "and I throw in the squash."

"Make it four and the squash is a gift," Ruby said, "because you'd have to carry it home."

He laughed and held out the basket. "Deal. Adam Smith would be proud of you, though he'd charge you the seven."

"Adam Smith never met a cat backpack," said Ruby, and handed over the money.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: A metal wire's resistance rises as it heats up, so Ohm's law gives a steady resistance only while the wire's temperature stays the same.
story:
The voltmeter read 2.4 volts, the ammeter 0.30 amps, and Landon wrote both numbers in his lab notebook before the moment could escape him. Ms. Siddiqui had promised the equipment cart to another class at the end of the period, which left him and Simran only twenty minutes to measure the resistance of the thin coiled wire stretched between two clamps. Divide voltage by current, she had said at the start, and you retrieve the resistance. It was supposed to be the easiest lab of the term.

Their first answer was eight ohms, and Landon felt the small satisfaction of a locked door swinging open. Then Mikaella leaned over from the next station, frowning at her own notebook. "Ours keeps coming out different every time we measure," she said. "Yours too? Simran, read it again."

Simran touched the probes to the wire and counted under his breath. "2.5 volts. 0.29 amps." He did the division twice. "It's above eight now. Almost nine." Landon wrote it down, then crossed it out, then wrote it again in the margin. Either their hypothetical perfect meter was lying, or something between the clamps was changing, something no one could see.

"Maybe the connections are loose," Simran said, and spent two full minutes tightening every clamp while Landon timed him. The reading after that was higher still. Simran sat back on his stool, defeated. "The meter's broken, then. We should just ask for another one."

Landon didn't answer. He was watching the wire itself, the dull grey coil sitting so quietly between the clamps, and he thought about how the numbers only crept upward, never down, and always faster the longer they kept the current flowing. He pulled his sleeve over his hand and touched the coil, quick, like testing an iron. It was warm. It had not been warm at the start.

"It's heating up," he said slowly. "The whole time we've been measuring, it's been getting warmer, and the resistance has been getting bigger." He flipped back through his notebook, and there it was, a perfect symmetry: each new reading higher than the last, in step with every minute the current ran. "So Ohm's law still works. It just gives you a steady resistance only while the wire stays the same temperature."

Mikaella was already writing on her hand. "Cold readings first, then hot ones," she said. "We graph both." Simran retrieved a cup of water from the sink, dunked the coil, and clipped the probes back on. The voltmeter settled at 2.4, the ammeter at 0.30. "Eight ohms," he said. "Welcome back."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Judgment words such as best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signs that a sentence expresses an opinion.
story:
The bus had not even left the school parking lot when Louis pulled his crumpled assignment sheet out of his backpack. Ms. Yang had given their class a stack of product reviews and a highlighter, and she had said only one thing about the task before the bell rang: "Trust the words themselves." Now, sitting three rows from the back with his knees pressed against the seat in front, he stared at a review of a basketball shoe and wondered what he was supposed to be trusting.

Ian leaned over from the aisle seat. "You done yet? I highlighted, like, all of it." His page was so saturated with yellow that it glowed, every sentence painted solid.

"You can't highlight everything," Louis said. "Then it means nothing." He looked down at his own page again. The words that Ian's highlighter had covered were jumping out at him now: best, worst, boring, beautiful, should. They kept appearing, over and over, in the sentences that felt like somebody talking, not like facts he could look up. "This shoe is the best guard shoe ever made." He could not check that. Nobody could.

Fanny turned around from the row in front of them. "What are you two arguing about?" Her braids swung as she twisted to see.

"Louis thinks I did it wrong," Ian said.

"Ms. Yang's example yesterday," Fanny said slowly. "Remember? Judgment words. She called them opinion words, I think. Best, worst, boring, beautiful, should. They're signs. Signs of an opinion."

Louis felt something click, like a small fracture running through his old plan and splitting it open. He grabbed his highlighter. "That's the rule. Those five words. Best, worst, boring, beautiful, should." He read down his page hunting for them. "'The most beautiful colorway.' Opinion. 'It should fit true to size.' Opinion. But 'the sole is two inches thick,' that one I could measure. That's not a judgment word." He highlighted only his five words, and the page came out striped instead of solid, clean and sparse next to Ian's blazing yellow brick.

Ian frowned at his own paper, then at Louis's. "So I got every sentence that had any feeling in it."

"You got every sentence, period," Fanny said, but not meanly.

The bus rattled over the tracks by the water tower, and Louis held both pages up side by side. On his, a pattern showed: the yellow marks clustered at the start and end of the review, where the writer got excited, and thinned out in the middle, where the specs were. Maybe the person who wrote it liked the shoe more than the shoe deserved. Or maybe it really was that good. He could not tell yet, and that bothered him in a good way, like a question he actually wanted to answer.

"Tomorrow," he said, "I'm going to count them. Every judgment word in every review. If one writer uses way more of them than the others, that tells us something."

Ian shrugged. "Sounds permanent, your new system."

"It's not permanent. It's just today's." Louis slid the papers into his folder, clicked the cap onto his highlighter, and watched the water tower slide out of view.

"Five words," Fanny said, holding up one hand, fingers spread. "You're sure that's all of them?"

Louis looked at his hand, then at hers. "Find me a sixth one on the bus and I'll buy you a snack."

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: French has a "near future" made with the verb "aller" plus an infinitive: "Je vais voyager" means "I am going to travel."
story:
Jessica sat at the kitchen table with her French notebook open to a page that still had nothing on it but the heading Mes projets pour l'année prochaine. The assignment was due tomorrow, one paragraph about her plans for next year, and Mr. Fischer had underlined the words future tense twice on the sheet. Her pencil hovered, then landed, and she wrote her first try: "Je voyagerai en Espagne avec ma famille." It looked stiff even to her, like a sentence wearing a suit.

She texted Maisie, who was doing the same assignment across the street. Five minutes later Maisie was at the door with her own notebook and a granola bar, and the two of them spread out over the table like they were planning a heist.

"I did mine already," Maisie said, turning her page around. "Je vais visiter mes grands-parents. Je vais nager tous les jours. Je vais apprendre à cuisiner."

Jessica read it twice. "That's not even a future word. Vais is the verb aller. That means to go."

"So? Mr. Fischer said we could use it. Watch this." Maisie pulled up a video on her phone, a clip from their class website, and in it a woman said "Je vais voyager en France cet été" while a suitcase spun on the screen.

Jessica sat back. The sentence meant "I am going to travel," she was sure of that, but it was built out of to go plus another verb. She looked down at her own paragraph, all stiff voyagerai and étudierai endings, and a suspicion began to form. Maybe French had two ways to talk about the future, and maybe one of them sounded more natural, the way people in English said "I'm gonna" instead of "I shall." It was a pattern she couldn't see directly, only its shadow, so she decided to test it.

"Call Aubree," she said. "She actually talks to her cousin in French."

Aubree put her cousin on speaker. When Jessica read "Je voyagerai en Espagne," there was a pause, then a laugh that made her cheeks go hot with embarrassment. When Maisie read "Je vais visiter mes grands-parents," the cousin said it sounded like something from a movie trailer. "For plans," Aubree translated, "we say je vais plus the verb. Always."

"That's the near future," Maisie said, pointing at her own page like it was a trophy.

Jessica erased nothing. Instead she wrote a new paragraph underneath the old one, converting each stiff sentence into the softer one: "Je vais étudier l'espagnol. Je vais rejoir l'équipe de natation." The words went faster now, like her pencil had figured out the rule before her brain did. When she read the whole paragraph out loud, it sounded like someone talking, not someone performing.

"One more line," Maisie said, stealing a corner of the granola bar. "What are you actually going to do next year?"

"Je vais écrire un roman," Jessica said. "Page one starts tonight."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In farsightedness, light focuses behind the retina, so near objects look blurry, and it is corrected with convex lenses.
story:
Aria waited on the low wall by the swings with her new glasses still folded in her hand, because wearing them felt like walking into a room where everybody could stare. Across the playground, Violet was flipping a bottle onto the picnic table, missing every time, and Aria could now read the brand name on the bottle from thirty feet away, which was almost worse than not being able to.

"Put them on," Autumn said, dropping onto the wall beside her. "I had to last year. You survive."

Aria slid them on. The chain-link fence snapped into single wires. The cracks in the pavement became distinct and interesting, and she could see Violet's expression when the bottle missed again, an acute look of betrayal. "Okay," Aria said. "Okay, that's a lot."

Then Violet jogged over to grab the bottle, and Aria noticed something strange. Through her own lenses, Violet's eyes looked smaller, like buttons on a shirt pulled tight. But last week, when Aria had borrowed Autumn's glasses to try them, Autumn's eyes had looked bigger, magnified, huge and startled. Same playground, same afternoon light. Two pairs of glasses, opposite effects. Aria sat with that puzzle while the swings squeaked and the coach blew a whistle for the soccer game nobody was really playing.

"You're staring at my face," Violet said.

"Your eyes look tiny. But when I tried Autumn's glasses, her eyes looked giant." Aria pulled the glasses off and held them up to the light the way her mother had held them in the optometrist's office two days ago. She remembered the room clearly now, where the doctor had slid different lenses into the big metal frame and asked which was better, one or two, and where her mother, in the corner chair, had gone quiet when the bill was handed over. Aria remembered deciding, in that chair, that one or two, the one that made the letters on the screen sharpen out of gray fuzz, was worth the money even if her stomach had tightened.

"My glasses fix farsightedness," Autumn said, squinting at the sky because her allergy was acting up and she was trying not to rub her eyes. "Near stuff is blurry for me. The light focuses behind the retina, my uncle told me, and my lenses are convex, so they fix it."

Aria turned that over. Convex, meaning curved outward, the kind that made things look bigger. Hers must be the opposite kind, the kind that made things look smaller, because her problem was the far stuff, not the near. She tested it right there on the wall. She held Autumn's glasses over the schedule taped to the fence post, and the small print swelled huge and doubled at the edges. She held her own over it and the letters shrank, clear but small. Cause and effect, two directions, like turning a tap one way to regulate the water hotter and the other way colder.

"So we're opposites," Aria said, and almost laughed. Autumn grinned, Violet rolled her now-tiny-looking eyes, and for a minute it felt like a club with two members.

But at the corner of her vision, through the sharp new lenses, Aria could see Ms. Buchanan on yard duty, watching her and writing something on a clipboard, and she knew the note was probably about yesterday, when Aria had claimed she couldn't see the whiteboard and had copied off Violet instead. Some things the glasses would fix. The rest she'd have to carry herself. She pushed them up her nose, hopped off the wall, and went to go see what the clipboard said.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break.
story:
Nora lay on the living room couch with her right arm propped on a pillow, the new cast already itching in three places she could not reach. Her grandfather, who had fallen off a ladder last week trimming the hedge, sat in the armchair with his own cast running from wrist to elbow. Between them on the coffee table sat a bowl of popcorn, which her mother had left with two spoons because neither of them could manage a handful.

"Six weeks," Nora said, reading the paper the doctor had given her. "You?"

"Ten, maybe twelve," her grandfather said. "They'll check the X-ray and decide."

Nora frowned at that. His break sounded worse than hers, but not that much worse. "That's strange. Yours is just the radius too, like mine. Why would yours take almost twice as long?"

"Old wood takes longer to set," he said, and shrugged.

Nora didn't buy it. She pulled her phone out with her left hand and typed with one thumb, awkward but workable, while her grandfather tried to scoop popcorn with his spoon and mostly succeeded in flicking kernels onto the carpet. The doorbell rang, and Alyson let herself in a moment later, as she had been doing every day since the accident, usually with snacks.

"I brought gummy worms," Alyson announced, "and I already opened them, sorry, my brother was going to obstruct the whole bag if I didn't." She dropped onto the couch beside Nora. "What are you googling?"

"Bones." Nora turned the screen toward her. "Look. Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones. So kids usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break." She read it aloud slowly, testing it. "So it's not just the break. It's the age."

"I could have told you that," her grandfather said. "I'm a slow healer. Your grandmother calls me a pessimistic patient because I always assume the worst."

"That's not the same thing at all," Nora said, laughing.

She sat up straighter, an idea forming. "Okay, let's test it. Grandpa, when you broke your wrist at sixteen, working at the garage, how long was the cast on?"

He thought about it, spoon paused in the air. "Five weeks, I believe. Maybe four and a half."

"And now, same kind of break, ten weeks." Nora wrote the numbers on a napkin with her left hand, the letters wobbly and huge. "Same person, same bone, different ages. That's the whole pattern right there."

"So mine comes off sooner partly because I'm fourteen," Nora said, "not because my doctor is being nice about it."

"Six weeks, minus good behavior," her grandfather said, wiggling his spoon at her. "So no climbing the bookshelf to rescue anything, even if it's very important."

"It was a school amendment," Nora said. "I agreed to no more shelves." She held up her good hand solemnly, and Alyson high-fived it, popping a gummy worm into her own mouth at the same time.

Her grandfather managed a spoonful of popcorn at last and raised it like a toast. "To the fastest bones in the room."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
The piano in Mr. Dela Cruz's garage had a cloth over it and a smell of dust and motor oil. He had told Ivy she could practice on it every Saturday if she kept the door open, and today was her third lesson on her own. She set her notebook on the bench and played the C major scale the way he had shown her, but her left hand kept landing one key short at the top.

She tried the scale six more times. Six times her thumb came down where a white key should have been and hit air. "Maybe the piano is missing keys," she said out loud, because nobody was there to hear her sound silly. The garage was sparse, just the piano, a workbench, and a shelf of paint cans, so she could see right away that no keys had fallen on the floor.

Ivy decided to document the problem before she fixed it. In her notebook she wrote the date, then began counting from the bottom. Her finger touched each white key as she counted aloud. "Fifty-two," she said at the top. Then she counted the black keys, jumping her hand up and down the groups of twos and threes. "Thirty-six." She added the two numbers in the margin. Eighty-eight. She had read in her library book that a standard modern piano has 88 keys, 52 white and 36 black, so the piano was whole. The problem was not the piano. It was her.

But why did her hand go wrong only near the top? She played the scale once more, slowly, and watched her fingers instead of the keys. Near the top there were two black keys in a row, then a gap, then three black keys. At the bottom of the scale there had been three, then a gap, then two. The pattern had flipped while she wasn't looking, and her hand had memorized the wrong map. She had been leaping the same gap all the way up, like climbing stairs that change height halfway.

She tested it. Starting at the top, she played the scale downward, watching each group of black keys before her fingers moved. Her thumb landed on white every time. She played it upward again, slower, saying "two, then three" under her breath at each group. No air, no wrong note.

At home she opened the spreadsheet she had started as a database of practice problems, with columns for date, problem, cause, and fix. She typed a new row: missed notes at top of scale; pattern of black keys changes; count groups before playing. She would show it to Mr. Dela Cruz next Saturday.

The next Saturday he stood in the garage doorway with a mug of coffee and listened to her play the scale up and down without a single mistake. When she finished, he nodded at the notebook in her lap.

"Read me the last row," he said.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
The note from Mr. Luo was folded into Muhammad's pocket so many times it had gone soft. He pulled it out again under the flagpole and read it for the fourth time: "Muhammad, thank you for helping me carry the science fair boards all week. Please come for dinner Friday at six o'clock, apartment 8B. Bring nothing but yourself. Sincerely, Mr. Luo."

"He said bring nothing," said Mariana, reading over his shoulder. "So why are you carrying a bag?"

Muhammad lifted the paper bag with the wrapped honey jar inside. "At my house you never visit someone empty-handed. My mom would call it embarrassing. He said I don't have to bring anything, but he didn't say I can't."

Isaak jogged up with his backpack bouncing. "You two are going to be late. His building is the tall one on Miller Street, and it's five fifty-two already. Also, Muhammad, your mom says be polite at dinner, don't just say hi and run."

They reached the lobby at five fifty-eight. Muhammad pressed the button for the elevator, and when the doors opened he stepped in first, holding the honey jar like it was volatile, as if one bump could ruin everything. Then he stopped and stared at the panel of buttons. One, two, three, five, six, seven, eight. He counted again, in case his eyes had skipped one. They had not.

"There's no four," he said.

"There's a five," said Isaak. "Just press it."

"But apartment 8B is on the eighth floor, and the floors still go up in order. Unless..." Muhammad traced the buttons with his finger. "Unless this building skips the fourth floor on purpose. Like, there's no fourth floor at all. The button isn't broken. It was never there."

Mariana pressed eight. "My grandmother's building in Manila has a different thing. You don't open gifts in front of the giver, or the giver feels watched. So if Mr. Luo opens your honey right now, don't be surprised if it's a little awkward, and don't be surprised if he waits, either."

The doors opened on the eighth floor, and there in the hallway was a door marked 8B. Muhammad knocked twice, then wondered if that was too soft, and knocked again harder. Mr. Luo opened the door with a smile and both hands extended, which Muhammad understood meant he should shake with his right hand while Mr. Luo held his forearm, a greeting warmer than any Muhammad got at school.

"You found us," said Mr. Luo. "Even with the missing floor?"

"There's no button for four," said Muhammad. "Why?"

Mr. Luo laughed. "In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor."

Muhammad handed over the paper bag quickly, before his nerve could fail. "It's honey. From my grandmother's village. I know you said bring nothing, but in my family we don't go anywhere without something."

Mr. Luo took the bag with both hands and did not open it. He set it on the shelf by the door, still wrapped, and Muhammad remembered what Mariana had said and felt his ears go warm with relief. At the table there were more rules to watch for, and Muhammad watched all of them: he waited until Mr. Luo picked up his chopsticks first, he turned his teacup with two fingers when it was refilled, and he made sure not to stick his chopsticks upright in his rice, because he had once seen Mr. Luo wince at a photo of exactly that.

At six forty, with the dishes being carried out, Muhammad saw the framed paintings along the kitchen wall. Each one depicted a different floor number, painted in careful brushstrokes, and between the three and the five there was a small square of blank paper.

"Is that where the four would be?" he asked.

Mr. Luo nodded once, and hung the blank square a little straighter.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: In meeting procedure, a quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the group's decisions to count.
story:
Hudson stood at the front of Kalia's living room holding his clipboard like a shield. The Garden Club was his to run today, because Kalia had appointed him president while she was stuck at her grandmother's, and he had promised to follow the agenda she left him: call to order, old business, budget vote, new business. The budget vote was the big one. The club had twenty dollars, and half the members wanted to spend it on seeds to pollinate the school's vegetable bed, while the others wanted insulation wrap to protect the water pipes of the rooftop garden over winter.

Only three people had arrived by four o'clock: Ariana, a boy named Max from another class, and Hudson himself. The clock ticked past four fifteen. Ariana kept glancing at the door, but Max was in a hurry and kept pushing. "We're here, we're a meeting, let's vote," he said. "Seeds. Done." Hudson looked down at the agenda. Kalia had written one word at the top in parentheses that he hadn't noticed before: quorum. He didn't know what it meant, but under it she had written "6 of 10."

"So we can't vote with three," Ariana said, reading over his shoulder. "It says six of ten."

"Where does it say that?" Max demanded. "Who made that rule?"

Hudson thought about it. It wasn't Kalia's rule, exactly. It was like a rule of the game, the same way you couldn't score a basket from out of bounds even if the ball went in. A quorum was the minimum number of members who had to be present for the group's decisions to count. Without that number, a vote was just three people talking in a living room. He tested the idea out loud. "If we vote now and seven people walk in and hate it, the vote doesn't count anyway. So voting early doesn't actually save time. It just starts an argument."

Max groaned but sat back down. Hudson went down the agenda item by item, and to keep the meeting from feeling dead, he asked each of the three of them to report one thing. Ariana described the turbulent wind that had knocked over the tomato cages on Tuesday, and Max admitted he had never actually watered his assigned bed, and Hudson wrote both things in the minutes so nothing got lost.

At four forty, the doorbell rang twice in a row. Four more members crowded in, shaking rain off their jackets, and Ariana counted heads out loud: seven. Hudson's stomach did a small flip. "We have a quorum," he said. "Budget vote, item three. Seeds or insulation. One at a time, everyone gets a turn to speak."

Ariana raised her hand first.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: The bystander effect is the finding that people are less likely to help when many others are watching, because each person assumes someone else will act.
story:
Hayden had been practicing the same skateboard trick for three weeks, and the playground's cracked basketball court was the only place flat enough to try it, which was how he happened to be leaning on the fence when the trouble started. A crowd of maybe fifteen kids had gathered near the swings, and in the middle of it stood Gloria, holding her drawing pad against her chest while a boy named Dex made loud comments about her picture of a horse. "It looks like a cow with anxiety," Dex announced, and the crowd laughed in that uncertain way crowds do, and nobody moved.

Hayden's feet stayed planted. That was the strange part. He wanted to help, he liked Gloria fine, and yet his sneakers seemed glued to the asphalt. So did everyone else's. He scanned the circle: Macie was there, chewing her sleeve; two sixth graders were checking their phones; a kid Hayden didn't even know was staring at his own shoes like they'd suddenly become controversial. Fifteen witnesses, zero helpers. Hayden's brain started to itch, the way it did during math when a pattern was hiding in a word problem.

Then the crowd shifted, and he could see Macie mouthing something to herself, over and over. She wanted to be the funny one, that was her whole reputation, and being funny meant jokes, and jokes were dangerous ground when Dex was already telling them. That gave Hayden an idea, quick and a little sneaky. He pushed off the fence, rolled his skateboard toward Macie, and when it bumped her foot he called out, "Macie! Show them the tsunami trick, the one where the board shoots up your leg!"

Macie brightened instantly. A performance meant her joke had a safe home. She launched into an exaggerated, terrible trick attempt that wiped out in the grass, and half the crowd wandered over to watch, groaning and cheering. That left only four kids around Gloria and Dex. Four witnesses instead of fifteen. And the moment the crowd thinned, a small fifth grader Hayden had barely noticed walked straight up to Gloria and said, "I want to see the horse."

Dex glanced around, found no audience, mumbled something about cows, and drifted off toward the water fountain. Gloria opened her pad. "It's an Arab stallion," she said, and her chin came back up to its usual height.

Later, on the bus, Hayden sat with Macie and pieced it out aloud. "Fifteen people, nobody moves. Four people, somebody moves in two seconds." Macie shrugged, still glowing from her wipeout. "My brother calls that the bystander effect," she said. "Everybody figures somebody else will do it." Hayden turned that over like a coin in his pocket, and decided he would cherish it, mostly so that next time he'd be the small fifth grader instead of the fence. For now, though, he had a promise to keep. "Saturday," he told Macie, "you teach me the tsunami trick, and I'll teach you to fall without dying." Macie stuck out her hand, and they shook on it right there over the rattling seats.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Labeling each moving box with the room it belongs in and its contents makes unpacking faster, because boxes can be carried straight to the right place.
story:
The last box thumped onto the floor of Leah's new room, and the movers were gone before she found the one thing she needed most. "My sheets have to be in here somewhere," she muttered, prying open a box marked in her mom's handwriting: MISC. It contained a toaster, a snow globe, and three paperbacks. Not sheets. She tried two more boxes in the hallway, both labeled MISC, and got a tangle of extension cords and a lamp shade. By nine o'clock she was sleeping in her sleeping bag on the bare mattress.

At her new school the next morning, a girl with a bright eccentric backpack covered in enamel pins sat down beside her. "I'm Calista. Boston said you moved here from Millbrook, so I'm officially forming a welcoming alliance with you. That means you get half my pizza at lunch." Boston, from the next row, leaned over. "Did your movers lose your stuff? My cousin's did." "No," Leah said slowly. "It's all in the house. It's just that my mom labeled every single box with the same word." She hadn't thought about it until she said it out loud, and the thought stuck with her through math and lunch and the whole bus ride home.

She tested the idea that afternoon. In the garage, thirty-odd boxes waited, nearly all of them shouting MISC. She dismantled her old system, which was to say she crossed out her mom's labels with a marker and wrote new ones: KITCHEN, DISHES. LEAH'S ROOM, SHEETS. LEAH'S ROOM, BOOKS. BATHROOM, TOWELS. It took over an hour, and her hand cramped, but when her mom came home and saw, she admitted it might have been a mistake to write MISC on everything. "Movers carry boxes straight to the right room if the box says the room," Leah said. "Ours just said nothing, so they all got dumped in the garage."

The next Saturday, Boston and Calista arrived with a hand truck they had borrowed from Boston's grandfather. Boston hauled boxes while Calista called out destinations like a train conductor, and Leah checked each label. Every box went to the right room in one trip. Nobody searched, nobody opened anything twice. By lunch the kitchen was unpacked, and by dinner Leah's room looked like a room.

That night she pulled the fitted sheet from the box marked LEAH'S ROOM, SHEETS, snapped it over the mattress, and climbed under a real blanket for the first time in a week. Her phone buzzed on the windowsill. Calista had sent a photo of the empty pizza box with three names signed inside the lid, and underneath it one message: "Same time next Saturday?"

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
The scoreboard above the practice ice showed Oliver's team losing 4 to 2, but Oliver was not watching the score. He was watching the shots counter, which read 23 to 9 in their favor. His father always said the score was the only number that mattered, but Oliver had started to wonder. Twenty-three shots and two goals, against nine shots and four. There had to be a reason hiding under those numbers.

"You're doing the face again," said Khadijah, dropping onto the bench beside him with her tablet. She ran the stats segment for the school's morning announcements, and she needed something good this week, because Mr. Sadeghi had hinted that the eighth-grade media club might retire the segment if nobody watched it. "The thinking face."

"Twenty-three shots," Oliver said. "Two goals. Their goalie is saving everything and ours is having a reckless night, just throwing himself around the crease. But is our shooting bad, or is their goalie good? How do you even squish all that into one number?"

Khadijah stopped typing. "That's it. That's my segment." She pulled up a football site and turned the screen toward him. "Look at this. They rate quarterbacks with one number. But here's the part that's going to drive you crazy." She tapped the top of a chart. "A perfect rating isn't a hundred."

Oliver stared. "That's ridiculous. Perfect should be a hundred. Everybody knows perfect is a hundred."

"That's what my cousin said on the couch last Sunday, and nobody could answer him. He plays peewee football and he was genuinely upset." She scrolled. "It's called passer rating. It takes all the passing numbers and combines them into one score, on a scale from zero up to one hundred fifty-eight point three."

"One fifty-eight point three," Oliver repeated slowly. His eyes went back to the shots counter, then to the ice, where the kid wearing his brother's old number took a shot from a bad angle that the goalie swallowed easily. "So every number in sports is like that. Somebody chose a formula and pressed a whole season down into one little figure, and then everybody argues about it like it's the truth."

"Exactly," Khadijah said. "Now help me test something, because I want my segment to say something nobody else says." She opened a blank page. "Give me your shots and your goals, period by period, from the last three games. You keep them in that notebook, don't pretend you don't."

He did keep them. They sat through the third period building a little table, and when they divided his team's shooting percentage by period, a pattern jumped out at him. The percentage was fine in every period except the second, when it collapsed. "We're not a bad shooting team," he said, tapping the page. "We're a bad between-periods team. Something happens in that locker room, or we come out flat, I don't know what yet. But the season average hides it completely. The average says we're okay."

The buzzer sounded, 5 to 3, and the players drifted off toward the benches. Oliver's brother skated past the gate, shaking off his gloves, and Oliver waved him over. "Hey. In the second period, do you feel different? Like tired, or like nobody's talking?"

His brother leaned on the boards, breathing hard. "Honestly? Everyone checks their phones at intermission. Coach keeps saying it kills our motivation, but nobody listens." He glanced at the tablet in Khadijah's hands, at the table glowing there in the cold rink light. "What's all that?"

"That," Oliver said, "is your second period."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
Mr. Kaminski held up Aiden's poster board for the class to see, and Aiden wished he hadn't. The caption under the photo read: The hunters taught an Inuit how to read the ice. Mr. Kaminski didn't say anything was wrong with it. He only asked, "Before we pin these up at the community centre, does anyone want to check their captions one more time?"

Aiden squinted at his own writing from the third row. Something about that sentence had started to itch at him on the bus that morning, a feeling he couldn't quite name, the way a word you write too many times starts to look bizarre. He remembered the article he'd used for research. It had said the man in the photo was one person, a single person, from a whole people. But the article had used a different word for him. Aiden had skipped past it, thinking it was a typo.

During partner talk, he leaned toward Lilya, who sat beside him. "Quick test," he said. "If I say 'an Inuit,' what does that sound like to you?"

Lilya turned her poster around. Her caption read: A storyteller, an Inuk, shares a legend with her grandchildren. "It sounds like a whole people got shrunk into one person," she said. "Inuktitut has the singular covered. One person is an Inuk. Inuit means 'the people.'" She tapped her page. "My grandmother would notice in half a second."

Aiden felt his ears go warm. He hadn't known that. He flipped back through his notes and found the line, plain as anything, in the third paragraph of the article he'd skimmed. His highlighter had sailed right over it. "So I basically wrote 'a people taught the people how to read the ice.'"

"Basically," Rita said from across the aisle, not unkindly. She held up her own caption, where she had written a list of holidays and, next to it, a note asking, Is this how my family would say it, or how a website says it? "I called my grandma last night to check. She disclosed more in ten minutes than the whole internet did."

Mr. Kaminski walked the rows, listening. When he reached Aiden's desk, Aiden said, "Can I fix mine before we hang them up? I want to get the word right, and I want to check one more thing in the article, the part about the school where the photo was taken."

"That's the whole point of a second look," Mr. Kaminski said.

At lunch, Aiden and Lilya sat with the poster between their trays. He crossed out the caption with a single clean line and wrote: The hunters taught an Inuk how to read the ice. Then, underneath, in smaller letters, he added a second line for the display: Inuktitut is the language, Inuit means "the people," and the man in the photograph is Mr. Uttak.

Lilya read it over his shoulder. "Now the kids at the centre will learn two things from one picture."

"And I learned three," Aiden said, and capped his pen.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: As a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.
story:
Penelope sat in the exam room with her arm propped on her lap, the fiberglass cast already looking less shiny than it had two weeks ago. On the wall hung a poster about how bones mend, and on the counter sat a folder that she was fairly sure contained her X-rays. She wanted to see them. She had fractured her radius falling off Remy's skateboard, and ever since, one question had been circling in her head: how did a bone glue itself back together when nobody had touched the broken ends?

She was still wondering when the door opened and the doctor came in, holding the X-ray films up to the light. "Want to see something interesting?" the doctor asked, and clipped the new film beside the old one from the day of the break. Penelope leaned close. In the first picture the bone was a clean line with a sharp gap in it, like a snapped chopstick. In the second, right at the break, there was a fuzzy lump, a cloudy little bridge joining the two ends.

"What is that?" Penelope asked.

"That's the callus," the doctor said. "It's a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends." Then the doctor checked her fingers, asked her to squeeze, and wrote something in the folder, leaving Penelope staring at the films.

So that was the hidden repair work. She had imagined the two ends snapping together like magnets, but instead her body had built scaffolding across the gap, invisible under the cast the whole time. She tried a small test, pressing her palm flat on the chair arm with her fingers perpendicular to the edge, then curling them slowly. They obeyed, which meant, she reasoned, that the lump was already letting the tendons work again. Maybe healing was less like fixing and more like an ecosystem inside her arm, lots of quiet processes consuming calcium and rebuilding, none of them visible from outside.

When she got home, Remy was waiting on the porch with a marker. "Sign my cast, everyone else did," Remy said, holding out the pen like it was a big deal, and Penelope noticed Remy had been signing every cast in class since September, collecting signatures the way some kids collect stickers. She wrote her name in careful letters along the plaster, right over the spot where the fuzzy bridge must be forming in the dark.

"Two more weeks," she said, "and they saw this off, and I get to see the callus again on one more X-ray."

"Can I come?" Remy asked. "I'll bring a better marker."
